payload.throughline: Separate what a person thinks, feels, and tends to do; then reason in both directions while keeping situational constraints and alternative causes visible.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: classify one belief statement. This low-stakes prompt is followed by the complete three-component model.
Purpose: you will be able to decompose an attitude into what a person believes, feels, and tends to do, then use agreement or conflict among those parts to make a bounded prediction.

The cognitive component contains beliefs or evaluations about an object. The affective component contains feelings and emotional reactions. The behavioral component contains action tendencies, intentions, or relevant actions toward the object.

When the components point in the same direction, the attitude is more internally aligned. When they conflict, a single attitude label hides useful information. Alignment can support behavioral consistency, but context and other determinants still matter.
Mental model — think, feel, tend to act: classify each observed statement first, mark its direction second, and only then evaluate alignment.

Think aloud: “Public transit reduces congestion” is a belief, so it is cognitive. “I enjoy riding the train” is affective. “I plan to buy a pass” is behavioral. Because all three are favorable, I call the attitude aligned; I do not claim the pass will certainly be purchased.

Worked case: a student believes exercise improves health, enjoys workouts, and schedules three sessions each week. The cognitive, affective, and behavioral evidence all point positively, so the attitude is aligned.

A second student endorses the health benefits but dislikes exercise and repeatedly avoids it. The positive cognitive component conflicts with negative affective and behavioral evidence, so the global label “positive attitude” is incomplete.
Guided practice: classify an explicitly emotional reaction without confusing it with a belief about consequences.
Less help: locate an intention within the three-component model.
On your own: inspect a short case for component mismatch and state which parts conflict.

Boundary: a report of what someone believes is not affect merely because it has a positive tone. A past action is not proof of a stable attitude, and aligned components do not remove situational constraints.
Near exit: classify three fresh statements and identify whether their evaluative directions align.
Changed-task exit: predict how selectively changing one component alters internal alignment while the other two remain fixed.
Repair the classification function: ask whether the evidence is a proposition, a feeling, or an action tendency before judging its direction.
Fresh re-entry: classify a new three-statement case with different content and no repeated answer.
Repair the alignment function: hold two components constant, change only the named component, and compare the before-and-after pattern.
Fresh re-entry: apply that same selective-change reasoning to a different component and context.
Recap from memory: define cognitive, affective, and behavioral components, then explain why alignment supports but does not guarantee matching behavior.
Each failed function receives one targeted cue and one untouched re-entry. A second miss returns control without counting repair as exit success.
Starting check: identify a case in which behavior conflicts with a prior attitude. The full behavior-to-attitude mechanisms follow.
Purpose: you will be able to distinguish three pathways through which enacted behavior can precede and influence later attitudes.

Foot-in-the-door begins with agreement to a small request and is followed by a larger related request. Role-playing can shift attitudes as people enact and interpret a social role. Cognitive dissonance is discomfort from important inconsistency among cognitions or between behavior and attitude.

Dissonance can be reduced by changing behavior, changing an attitude, or adding a cognition that reconciles the inconsistency. When external justification for a counterattitudinal act is weak, internal attitude adjustment may become a stronger reduction route; the process is conditional, not guaranteed.

Mental model — sequence, pressure, reduction: small-then-large request suggests foot-in-the-door; enacted role suggests role-playing; aversive inconsistency followed by reconciliation suggests dissonance reduction.

Think aloud: a volunteer first signs a brief pledge and later accepts a related weekly task. The diagnostic cue is the two-request sequence, so I select foot-in-the-door rather than dissonance, because no internal conflict is required by the case.

Worked case: a participant freely writes a position they initially oppose and receives little external reward. The behavior conflicts with the prior attitude, creating dissonance. One possible reduction is shifting the attitude toward the written position.

Contrast case: an actor repeatedly performs the responsibilities of a supportive mentor and later reports warmer views toward mentoring. The enacted role, not a small-then-large request, supports a role-playing account.
Guided practice: recognize the small-request then larger-related-request structure.
Less help: identify role enactment as the behavior that precedes attitude change.
On your own: choose a direct dissonance-reduction route without assuming only one route exists.

Boundary: foot-in-the-door is not simply any compliance, role-playing is not merely observing a role, and dissonance does not mean every unpleasant feeling. Each mechanism requires its defining sequence.
Near exit: infer a likely attitude shift from a freely chosen counterattitudinal act with weak external justification.
Changed-task exit: identify the behavior-to-attitude process from a new multi-step request sequence rather than from internal discomfort.
Repair the dissonance function: locate the inconsistency, assess the external justification supplied, and choose a change that reduces conflict.
Fresh re-entry: apply the same weak-justification reasoning to a new counterattitudinal behavior.
Repair process selection: map small-then-large, enacted-role, and inconsistency-reduction cues before naming a process.
Fresh re-entry: classify a different enacted-behavior sequence without reusing the exposed request case.
Recap from memory: state the defining sequence for foot-in-the-door, role-playing, and cognitive dissonance, plus two possible dissonance-reduction routes.
One targeted mechanism cue is followed by one fresh function-matched item. Persistent uncertainty returns control without exit credit.
Starting check: compare a broad attitude with an attitude that names the exact action, setting, and time being predicted.
Purpose: you will be able to make conditional behavior predictions from attitudes while keeping the match between measures and the surrounding context explicit.

Attitudes are more informative when they are strong, accessible in memory, based on direct experience, and specific to the behavior being predicted. A broad attitude toward health is not the same predictor as an attitude toward attending a particular clinic next Tuesday.

Behavior also depends on opportunity, resources, norms, incentives, habits, and constraints. Removing a barrier can increase attitude-behavior correspondence; adding a strong barrier can reduce it. The attitude contributes to prediction but never guarantees one action.

Mental model — match, access, context: first match attitude and behavior at the same level of specificity, then inspect whether the attitude is accessible and whether the situation permits or opposes the action.

Think aloud: two people equally favor vaccination, but only one can reach the clinic before it closes. The opportunity difference changes the behavioral prediction even though the reported attitudes match.

Worked case: a person has a strong, readily recalled, firsthand positive attitude toward cycling to work tomorrow and has a safe route and bicycle available. Those aligned conditions support a higher probability of cycling.
If the bicycle is unavailable, the same attitude no longer implies the same behavior. The constraint moderates the link; it does not prove the attitude was false.
Guided practice: identify a situational constraint that blocks an attitude-consistent action.
Less help: recognize how direct experience and accessibility can strengthen the predictive role of an attitude.
On your own: distinguish an attitude effect from a norm or opportunity effect in a short case.
Boundary: attitude-behavior correspondence is not a personality certainty. A matching action does not prove attitude was the only cause, and a blocked action does not prove the attitude was absent.
Near exit: compare two people with the same stated attitude but different opportunities and predict the more likely behavior.
Changed-task exit: predict how removing a constraint alters attitude-behavior correspondence while attitude strength remains fixed.
Repair conditional prediction: match the attitude to the exact behavior, list the available opportunity and constraints, then make a relative rather than certain prediction.
Fresh re-entry: apply that comparison to a new behavior with strong, accessible, specific attitude evidence.
Repair context moderation: hold the attitude constant, change only the named situational factor, and compare the two behavioral probabilities.
Fresh re-entry: apply the same moderator isolation to a new norm or incentive change.
Recap from memory: name four attitude properties and four contextual factors that can change the attitude-behavior link, then state why the prediction remains probabilistic.
One context-focused cue and one untouched re-entry bound each exit function. Continued uncertainty returns control without awarding success.
